I'm posting this under v/politics because this topic has been highly discussed here, and it has obvious and far-reaching political implications. I haven't gone out of my way to raise this issue in the comments of the many threads that have been posted in the last few weeks regarding encryption, but I have been seriously wondering whether this topic isn't soon to be a moot point. If there is anyone on this board with some cryptography expertise, please speak up.

Recently it was [announced](http://www.dwavesys.com/press-releases/d-wave-systems-announces-general-availability-1000-qubit-d-wave-2x-quantum-computer) that quantum super computers are here, and solving problems--that would previously have taken conventional supercomputers thousands of years to solve--quite quickly. The kind of optimization problem these computers were engineered to solve have super-exponential complexity functions (the time it takes to solve them grows faster than any exponential function as the size of the problem increases -- O(n!) if not [O(n^(2^n))](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5209960/algorithms-with-superexponential-runtime) for my fellow geeks--yet they are being solved readily by these machines.

I studied complexity theory a little bit (I was focusing on graph theory) while I was working on my masters degree, and I have some basic knowledge of certain asymmetric encryption systems (eg RSA). It is my understanding that all of these encryption schemes rely on some math problem being very hard to solve (that is to say, there is no efficient algorithm to solve them). Quantum computers seem to be able to use *inefficient* algorithms to solve them quickly, because of the [unique way in which they work](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JhHMJCUmq28).

To me, this signals the end of the encryption schemes we currently use. However, I stumbled upon [this article](http://rubin.rub.de/en/cryptography-microdevices) which seems to be saying, "nah, we're good." Here's the thing though, the article linked in my previous sentence makes very little sense to me, and seems to be saying *nothing*. Does anyone here know enough about this subject to convince me that we can design math problems hard enough to thwart this new generation of quantum super-computers in ways that traditional computers can effectively utilize?

I'm going out on a limb here. Because we can't seem to build quantum computers yet. They my not ever work, but it's not even close right now. Hey, I'll put $10 on controlled power generating fusion first.

We have built them. They exist. We are solving hard problems with them.
